header.name: Introduction to Computational Complexity
header.description: One of the many beautiful results in the theory of computation is the equivalence of “deterministic” and “non-deterministic” variants of different models of computation, like Turing machines. One may ask whether this equivalence holds if we restrict the running time (or number of steps) of a Turing machine. This gives rise to one of the most important open problems in computer science, popularly known as the P versus NP question. This will be the starting point of our course. After briefly recalling Turing machines and discussing formal definitions of the classes ‘P’ and ‘NP’, we will see the notion of ‘reductions’, which will allow us to talk about the ‘hardest’ problems in NP, known as NP-complete problems. We will discuss some important NP-complete problems from different areas like logic, graph theory, etc. After that, we will briefly talk about other important classes corresponding to the running time of a Turing machine, like ‘co-NP’, ‘EXP’, and ‘NEXP’. Following this, we will see a classification of computational problems based on the space used by the Turing machine. We will discuss some important classes like PSPACE and NPSPACE (the space-variants of P and NP, respectively), their relations with P and NP, a ‘PSPACE-complete’ problem, the equivalence of PSPACE and NPSPACE, and other space complexity classes. Then, we will see the concept of ‘polynomial hierarchy’, which generalizes P, NP, and co-NP and is contained in PSPACE. If time permits, we will see a high-level introduction of randomness in computation.
